title: Domains: a strongly transcendental generator kills quasi-finiteness
statement: Let $R\subseteq S$ be a subring of a commutative ring with $R$ and $S$ integral domains (nonzero rings without zero divisors). Let $x\in S$ be strongly transcendental over $R$ [def-weil-pbc-strongly-transcendental] (for the inclusion $R\to S$; for domains this says that $a_0+a_1x+\dots+a_kx^k=0$ with $a_i\in R$ forces all $a_i=0$), and assume that $S$ is a finitely generated module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module] over the subring $R[x]\subseteq S$ generated by $R$ and $x$ (so $R\to S$ is of finite type [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra]). Then $R\to S$ is not quasi-finite at any prime ideal of $S$ [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime].

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00Q1 (lemma-domains-transcendental-not-quasi-finite, line 30666), stated there with '(strongly) transcendental'; tag verified in literature/stacks-project/tags/tags

proof.text: *Set-up.* Let $s_1,\dots,s_m\in S$ generate $S$ as a module over $R[x]$ [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. Every element of $R[x]$ is a polynomial expression in $x$ with coefficients in $R$, so every element of $S$ is a polynomial in $x,s_1,\dots,s_m$ with coefficients in $R$, and $R\to S$ is of finite type [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra]. Since $x$ is strongly transcendental over $R$ [def-weil-pbc-strongly-transcendental], taking $u=1$: if $\sum_ia_ix^i=0$ with $a_i\in R$ then all $a_i=0$. Hence the $R$-algebra map $R[X]\to R[x]$, $X\mapsto x$, from the polynomial ring [def-weil-polynomial-ring] is injective as well as surjective, so it is an isomorphism, and every element of $R[x]$ is $\sum_ia_ix^i$ with uniquely determined coefficients $a_i\in R$. Since $S$ is an integral domain, a nonzero $u\in S$ can be cancelled, so for domains strong transcendence is exactly this uniqueness of coefficients. The same remarks apply verbatim to any inclusion of domains $R_1\subseteq S_1$ with $x\in S_1$ strongly transcendental over $R_1$ and $S_1$ finitely generated over $R_1[x]$; they are used for $R_1\subseteq S_1$ equal to $R\subseteq S$ in steps 2-6 and to $R'\subseteq S'$ in steps 7-10.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00Q1 (lemma-domains-transcendental-not-quasi-finite, line 30666), proof (the hypotheses; the identification of R[x] with the polynomial ring is implicit in 'R[x] is normal')

proof.text: *Normal case: residue fields.* In steps 2-6 assume in addition that $R$ is a normal domain [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring], and suppose, to reach a contradiction, that $R\to S$ is quasi-finite at a prime $\mathfrak q\subset S$ [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime]. Put $\mathfrak p=R\cap\mathfrak q$, $F=S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ the fibre ring [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime], $j:S\to F$, $s\mapsto s\otimes1$, and $\mathfrak Q\subset F$ the prime with $j^{-1}(\mathfrak Q)=\mathfrak q$; by definition $\{\mathfrak Q\}$ is open in $\operatorname{Spec}F$. $F$ is a finite type $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$-algebra [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra], generated by $x\otimes1,s_1\otimes1,\dots,s_m\otimes1$ (step 1), since $s\otimes\lambda=\lambda\cdot(s\otimes1)$. By [lem-weil-pbc-isolated-prime-finite-type-algebra-residue-finite] (with $k=\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, $B=F$, the prime $\mathfrak Q$) the residue field $\kappa(\mathfrak Q)$ is a finite extension of $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-ring-primes-residue-fields] (2), $\psi_{\mathfrak q}:F\to\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ induces an isomorphism $\kappa(\mathfrak Q)\cong\kappa(\mathfrak q)$; as $\psi_{\mathfrak q}(1\otimes\lambda)=\bar\lambda$, this isomorphism is compatible with the maps from $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, so $\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ is a finite extension of $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ (via the map induced by $R\subseteq S$).

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00Q1 (lemma-domains-transcendental-not-quasi-finite, line 30666), proof, first paragraph: 'Assume that the extension kappa(p) ⊂ kappa(q) is finite. This would be the case if R → S is quasi-finite at q' (Lemma 00PJ (1) => (6) on the fibre)

proof.text: *The intermediate prime.* Let $\mathfrak r=R[x]\cap\mathfrak q$, a prime of $R[x]$ with $R\cap\mathfrak r=\mathfrak p$. The inclusions $R\subseteq R[x]\subseteq S$ induce field homomorphisms $\kappa(\mathfrak p)\to\kappa(\mathfrak r)\to\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] ($a/t\mapsto a/t$) whose composite is the map $\kappa(\mathfrak p)\to\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ of step 2. A field homomorphism is injective, so $\kappa(\mathfrak r)$ is a $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$-subspace of the finite-dimensional $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$-vector space $\kappa(\mathfrak q)$, and $\kappa(\mathfrak r)$ is a finite extension of $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00Q1 (lemma-domains-transcendental-not-quasi-finite, line 30666), proof, first paragraph: 'since kappa(p) ⊂ kappa(r) ⊂ kappa(q) we see that the extension kappa(p) ⊂ kappa(r) is finite too'

proof.text: *Going down.* $R[x]\cong R[X]$ (step 1) is a normal domain by [lem-weil-pbc-polynomial-ring-normal-domain], since $R$ is. $S$ is a finitely generated $R[x]$-module, hence integral over $R[x]$ by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-algebra-is-integral]. So $R[x]\subseteq S$ is an inclusion of domains with normal base and $S$ integral over it, and [lem-weil-pbc-going-down-normal-integral] (with $A=R[x]$, $B=S$, $\mathfrak p_A=\mathfrak pR[x]\subseteq\mathfrak p'_A=\mathfrak r$, which are primes by step 4, and $\mathfrak q'_B=\mathfrak q$, with $R[x]\cap\mathfrak q=\mathfrak r$) gives a prime $\mathfrak q_1\subseteq\mathfrak q$ of $S$ with $R[x]\cap\mathfrak q_1=\mathfrak pR[x]$. Then $R\cap\mathfrak q_1=R\cap\mathfrak pR[x]=\mathfrak p$ (step 4), and $\mathfrak q_1\neq\mathfrak q$ because $R[x]\cap\mathfrak q_1=\mathfrak pR[x]\neq\mathfrak r=R[x]\cap\mathfrak q$ (step 4).

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00Q1 (lemma-domains-transcendental-not-quasi-finite, line 30666), proof, first paragraph: Lemma 00H1 (here its domain form 030A) and going down, Proposition 00H8

proof.text:
*$\mathfrak q$ is not isolated in its fibre: the normal case.* By step 5, $\mathfrak q_1\subsetneq\mathfrak q$ are primes of $S$ both lying over $\mathfrak p$. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-ring-primes-bijection] there are primes $\mathfrak Q_1,\mathfrak Q$ of $F$ with $j^{-1}(\mathfrak Q_1)=\mathfrak q_1$, $j^{-1}(\mathfrak Q)=\mathfrak q$, and $\mathfrak Q_1\subsetneq\mathfrak Q$ (the bijection preserves and reflects inclusions). In the Zariski topology of $\operatorname{Spec}F$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum] an open set containing $\mathfrak Q$ is $\operatorname{Spec}F\setminus V(I)$ for an ideal $I$ with $I
ot\subseteq\mathfrak Q$; then $I
ot\subseteq\mathfrak Q_1$, so the open set also contains $\mathfrak Q_1
eq\mathfrak Q$. Hence $\{\mathfrak Q\}$ is not open, contradicting the assumption of step 2 that $R	o S$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q$ [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime]. Conclusion of steps 2-6 (*): for an inclusion of domains $R_1\subseteq S_1$ with $R_1$ a normal domain, $x\in S_1$ strongly transcendental over $R_1$ and $S_1$ finitely generated as an $R_1[x]$-module, $R_1	o S_1$ is not quasi-finite at any prime of $S_1$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00Q1 (lemma-domains-transcendental-not-quasi-finite, line 30666), proof, end of first paragraph: 'Hence the fibre ... contains a point not equal to q, namely q', whose closure contains q and hence q is not isolated in its fibre'

proof.text: *General case: the normalization.* Now drop the normality of $R$. Let $K$ and $L$ be the fields of fractions of $R$ and $S$. Every nonzero element of $R\subseteq S$ is invertible in $L$, so $a/b\mapsto ab^{-1}$ embeds $K$ into $L$ compatibly with $R\subseteq S\subseteq L$; regard $K\subseteq L$. Let $R'\subseteq K$ be the integral closure of $R$ in $K$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure]. By [lem-weil-pbc-integral-closure-algebraic-extension-normal] (with $P=R$ and the algebraic extension $L=K$ of $K$ there) $R'$ is a subring of $K$ containing $R$, integral over $R$, with field of fractions $K$, and a normal domain [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]. Let $S'\subseteq L$ be the subring generated by $R'$ and $S$: the set of finite sums $\sum_i\sigma_i\rho_i$ with $\sigma_i\in S$, $\rho_i\in R'$ (this set contains $1$ and is closed under sums and products). $S'$ is an integral domain (a subring of $L$), $R'\subseteq S'$ and $S\subseteq S'$, the square of inclusions $R\subseteq S\subseteq S'$, $R\subseteq R'\subseteq S'$ commutes (all are inclusions in $L$), and every element of $S'$ is a sum of products of an element of (the image of) $S$ and one of $R'$, i.e. $S\otimes_RR'\to S'$ is surjective.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00Q1 (lemma-domains-transcendental-not-quasi-finite, line 30666), proof, second paragraph: 'let R ⊂ R' ⊂ K be the integral closure ... Let S ⊂ S' ⊂ L be the subring ... generated by R' and S. Note that by construction the map S ⊗_R R' → S' is surjective'

proof.text: *The hypotheses for $R'\subseteq S'$.* (a) $x$ is strongly transcendental over $R'$ in $S'$ [def-weil-pbc-strongly-transcendental]: let $\sum_{i=0}^k\rho_ix^i=0$ in $S'$ with $\rho_i\in R'\subseteq K$. Choose a common denominator $d\in R\setminus\{0\}$ with $d\rho_i=r_i\in R$ for all $i$; multiplying by $d$ gives $\sum_ir_ix^i=0$ in $L$, hence in $S$, so all $r_i=0$ (step 1), and $\rho_i=r_i/d=0$. If $u\cdot\sum_i\rho_ix^i=0$ with $u\in S'$, then $u=0$ or $\sum_i\rho_ix^i=0$ since $S'$ is a domain, and in both cases $u\rho_i=0$ for all $i$. (The source leaves this unstated.) (b) $S'$ is generated as an $R'[x]$-module by $s_1,\dots,s_m$ [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]: an element of $S'$ is $\sum_i\sigma_i\rho_i$, and $\sigma_i=\sum_jc_{ij}s_j$ with $c_{ij}\in R[x]$, so $\sum_i\sigma_i\rho_i=\sum_j(\sum_ic_{ij}\rho_i)s_j$ with $\sum_ic_{ij}\rho_i\in R'[x]$. Hence $R'\subseteq S'$, $x$ satisfy the hypotheses of (*) in step 6, $R'$ being a normal domain by step 7.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00Q1 (lemma-domains-transcendental-not-quasi-finite, line 30666), proof, second paragraph: 'This implies that R'[x] ⊂ S' is finite'

proof.text: *$\operatorname{Spec}S'\to\operatorname{Spec}S$ is surjective.* Every $\rho\in R'$ is a root of a monic polynomial with coefficients in $R\subseteq S$ (step 7), so it is integral over $S$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure]. The elements of $S'$ integral over $S$ form a subring of $S'$ containing $S$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure]; it contains $R'$ and hence all sums $\sum_i\sigma_i\rho_i$, so it is $S'$: $S'$ is integral over $S$. As $S\to S'$ is injective, [lem-weil-pbc-integral-injective-lying-over] shows that for every prime $\mathfrak q\subset S$ there is a prime $\mathfrak q''\subset S'$ with $S\cap\mathfrak q''=\mathfrak q$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00Q1 (lemma-domains-transcendental-not-quasi-finite, line 30666), proof, second paragraph: 'the map S ⊂ S' induces a surjection on Spec, see Lemma 00GQ'

proof.text: *Conclusion by the four rings lemma.* Let $\mathfrak q\subset S$ be a prime and choose $\mathfrak q''\subset S'$ over it (step 9). Suppose $R\to S$ were quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q$ [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime]. $R\to S$ is of finite type (step 1), the square $R\to S\to S'$, $R\to R'\to S'$ commutes and $S\otimes_RR'\to S'$ is surjective (step 7), and the inverse image of $\mathfrak q''$ in $S$ is $\mathfrak q$; so [lem-weil-pbc-quasi-finite-four-rings] (with $R'$, $S'$ and the prime $\mathfrak q''$ of $S'$) says that $R'\to S'$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q''$. This contradicts (*) of step 6 applied to $R'\subseteq S'$ and $x$ (step 8). Hence $R\to S$ is not quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q$, for every prime $\mathfrak q$ of $S$.
